column3: Direct inverse household example: a righteous spouse does not transfer salvation.
Extends household and lineage context, but does not address separation from oppression.
Physical nearness to a house does not secure its sacred refuge.
Joins prayer and flight from a wrongful people, directly illuminating layered rescue.
Makes recompense answer to one's own deeds, excluding rescue through another's righteousness.
Depicts deliverance from enclosing danger and the responsibility that follows it.
Links Pharaoh's oppressive work and people to the reversal of the oppressed.
Places spousal pressure and divine permission within the surah's household setting.
Frames every hostile plan as held within divine knowledge, qualifying Pharaoh's apparent control.
Pharaoh's command to build contrasts his constructed power with the requested dwelling near God.
Affirms that outcomes are not misassigned, supporting responsibility for oppressive action.
Clarifies that the paired examples distinguish opposed commitments, not mere biography.
Introduces Pharaoh's wife within his household before her independent faithful stance.
Provides nearby household-law context without materially developing the focus reading.
Adds garden imagery as productive enclosure, supporting the requested garden's protective aspect.
Contrasts secure habitation with communal wrongdoing that turns it into fear.
Shows trust and disclosure tensions within a household, relevant to relational allegiance.
Supplies gardens as a protective outcome before the Lord, though it repeats later garden evidence.
Combines a decisive separation with rescue of a believing group from its opponents.
Broadens the household frame through spouses, descendants, and provision.
Shows divergent response within a shared setting, supporting non-transferable allegiance.
Names Pharaoh's people as an oppressive order from which rescue breaks a social bond.
Contrasts hostile spousal coalition with sustaining divine and believing support.
Presents mercy as selective rescue of believers from collective disgrace.
Opposes wrongful devotion with exclusion from the garden refuge.
Shares the surah's conflict and final-destination setting but adds little to the focus.
Shows gardens left behind by the drowned, distinguishing possessions from real safety.
Adds a woman's direct devotion and lineage setting that anticipates the next surah example.
Connects harm to prior deeds, but only indirectly to the focus's escape and dwelling.
Develops individualized, cumulative return for deeds, reinforcing personal moral agency.
Sets Pharaoh's challenge to divine lordship behind the focus's rejection of him.
Direct adjacent promise of repentance, garden entry, and protection for believers.
The phrase of nearness shifts protection from hostile proximity to divine proximity.
Depicts vulnerability before a wrongful people, without the focus's rescue or dwelling.
Supports divine nearness as an authoritative source rather than a spatial claim.
Explicitly gives thanks for rescue from a wrongful people after reaching safety.
Tests a chosen house as protection and finds it unable to bear the required refuge.
The following Marian example limits escape from oppressive ties from becoming rejection of all ties.
Shows mercy separating believers from an encompassing severe punishment.
Uses comparison and upright conduct, but offers no specific household or rescue development.
Directly measures marital relation by faith, devotion, repentance, and worship rather than status.
Shows political subjugation distorting a people's capacity to recognize truth.
Makes rescue include separation of a household from a wrongful practice and people.
Places forgiveness and punishment under divine sovereignty, but remains general.
Only a contrast route about lineage claims; it supplies no positive focus evidence.
Clarifies the force of Qur'anic examples generally, duplicating stronger example evidence.
Extends the surah's household responsibility and protection, with a contrary destination.
Selectively separates even one household: family membership does not determine deliverance.
Associates a believing household entry with an expanding network of faith-based belonging.
No clear addition to the focus's household, nearness, or rescue readings.
Building imagery is too remote from the requested divine dwelling.
Completes Moses's escape from the wrongful people by recognizing him as safe.
Individualized entitlement claims only distantly parallel personal moral standing.
Reiterates the excluded wife case, adding that household separation is measured rather than accidental.
Provides the Marian continuity that helps read the following example without extending the focus directly.
Treats a house as a protected communal center under its Lord, parallel to the requested dwelling.
Characterizes recurrent wrongdoing as a community-forming order, relevant to escape from the wrongful people.
Links faith and restorative deeds to enduring garden belonging.
Divine knowledge of hidden and public matters is broad background only.
Clarifies examples as instruments of understanding, redundant with nearer example cards.
Links faith, righteous deeds, and humble orientation to enduring garden belonging.
Distinguishes desire for garden entry from entitlement, but only indirectly.
Combines gardens, purified spouses, and nearness to the Lord in a durable alternative belonging.
Contrasts the wrongful outcome with believers' garden location near their Lord.
Its lineage route is marked contrast and provides no positive development of the focus.
Adds a protected garden outcome, but is redundant and not household-specific.
Secret contrary planning and divine record offer only remote parallel to household disclosure.
Contrasts a house functioning as confinement with the focus's requested protected dwelling.
Extends the Marian sequence and divine nearness, chiefly through the following example.
Shows collective false attribution and wrongful speech, only loosely related to Pharaoh's action.
Shares fire and belief themes but does not develop the focus's central relations.
Shows marital rupture managed without erasing moral and communal obligations.
A mercy-and-punishment boundary is a distant spatial parallel to rescue.
Sets limits on analogy-making, but adds little beyond stronger example cards.
Displays Pharaoh's people promising release under pressure, clarifying the oppressive collective context.
Treats denial as inherited community behavior, a general parallel to wrongful people.
A woman's public confession supplies a limited contrast in household moral agency.
Its rescue link is explicitly contrast, not positive support for the focus reading.
Divine knowledge and repudiated association are general background, not a focused parallel.
The only route is contrast evidence and does not support the focus positively.
Collective destruction supplies a broad consequence frame without the focus's rescue pattern.
Directly depicts believers being rescued from a collective calamity through prior restraint.
No distinct addition beyond the broader destruction context already present.
Only contrast evidence about lineage allocation; no positive focus contribution.
A hostile demand for punishment gives distant context for rejecting divine truth.
The positive trust reading is remote from the focus's household and rescue structure.
Adds a household scene of desire and social judgment, a limited relational parallel.
Depicts gardens as enduring shelter with purified spouses, supporting the alternative dwelling.
Shows heedless reception of speech, with no specific rescue or household addition.
Collective response can sustain rejection, but repeats the oppressive-community idea abstractly.
Fire and forced building are too unspecific to illuminate the focus beyond persecution imagery.
Defines salvation as passage out of punishment toward a protected alternative.
Sets a conflict between affiliation and enemy status, but not the focus's layered rescue.
Shows repeated deviation becoming settled unbelief, supporting personal rather than inherited alignment.
Shows harmful teaching can divide spouses, a limited negative household parallel.
Distinguishes secret counsel used for wrongdoing from counsel redirected to goodness and restraint.
Names fear of expulsion and loss of social order, but offers no actual rescue reading.
Protects believers from exclusion based on status, defining belonging through faith.
Shared call to restraint and obedience gives only general faith orientation.
Contrasts a passing material channel with what is with God as the enduring source.
Reinforces the Pharaoh oppression and rescue background already represented more directly elsewhere.
Places Mary in a divinely sustained protected setting, extending the following Marian boundary example.
Highlights Mary's election and purity, supplying background for the surah's final example.
Links faithful men and women with departure from homes and divine response to loss.
Directly joins the oppressed, including women and children, to prayer for exit from a wrongful town.
Makes remaining under wrongful conditions answerable while opening migration as release.
Preserves the case of those unable to leave, qualifying any simple demand for separation.
Portrays migration toward God as leaving an oppressive place for divine refuge and abundance.
Shows Pharaoh's ruling circle sustaining a collective program of oppression.
Restates rescue from Pharaoh's household system, though it is redundant with 14:6.
Sets Israel's escape against Pharaoh's final pursuit and collapse.
Commands Lot's household to depart while distinguishing the wife who remains.
Shows personal fidelity within a powerful household despite intimate coercion.
Frames withdrawal into hardship as preferable to surrendering personal moral agency.
Makes night departure with a household an explicit rescue from a condemned town.
Names relocation after wrongdoing as an earthly and final recompense.
Joins migration after trial to forgiveness and mercy, though less specifically than 4:75.
Completes Pharaoh's attempt at expulsion with the drowning of him and his force.
Uses withdrawal from a coercive religious setting to seek an alternative refuge.
Places Moses's earlier preservation and later flight within the Pharaoh narrative.
Commands a protected nocturnal departure from Pharaoh's pursuit.
Depicts relocation of Abraham and Lot to a blessed land as deliverance.
Gives Lot both judgment and rescue from a corrupt community.
Parallels the Marian preservation in 66:12, limiting the focus's separation reading.
Authorizes resistance for those wronged, giving a direct oppression context.
Names expulsion from homes without right, closely sharpening the requested divine dwelling.
Gives Mary and her son a settled, protected refuge, directly paralleling alternative belonging.
Orders Moses to lead his servants away, making collective departure from Pharaoh explicit.
States the rescue of Moses and all with him before the pursuers' destruction.
Selectively rescues Lot's household, reiterating the family-boundary pattern.
Again separates Lot's wife from the saved household, adding little beyond stronger parallels.
Names Pharaoh's structural domination, division, and targeting of a vulnerable group.
Joins Moses's departure to a request for guided direction after leaving Pharaoh's city.
Ends Pharaoh's power and forces in the sea, confirming the failure of oppressive action.
Shows Lot distressed within the corrupt town before the rescue distinction is made.
Treats God's earth as open for faithful action, supporting departure when a setting constrains it.
Centers a believer within Pharaoh's own people who keeps an independent faith position.
Explicitly saves that believer from Pharaoh's evil plot while judgment closes on the people.
Shows Pharaoh's people continuously exposed to the outcome of their oppressive order.
Records Pharaoh's territorial and river-based claim to sovereignty, contrasting divine nearness and refuge.
Introduces Pharaoh's people as a tested collective under a trustworthy messenger.
Explicitly states rescue of Israel from humiliating punishment.
Restricts the saved household in Lot's town to a single believing house.
Reiterates Lot-family rescue with the exception of the wife who remains behind.
Prioritizes faith allegiance over even the closest kinship ties.
Names believers expelled from homes who seek God's favor and support His cause.
Treats women crossing hostile allegiance lines as autonomous believers rather than transferable marital property.
Sets a direct covenant of women's moral agency apart from household relation.
Makes Pharaoh's claim to highest lordship an explicit opposite pole to the focus's appeal to God.
